name: P1 · Value Education
description: 5 of 8 topics so far (10 sets × 20 questions): Value Education – Basics; Teaching Methods of Value Education; Theories of Goodness; Rules and Principles of Human Behaviour; Theories of Behaviour. More topics are added to this pack as the plan goes on; re-importing only adds the new sets.

sets.name: 1 · Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics

questions.question: The word 'value' is derived from the Latin word 'valere', which means:

options.B: To be of worth, to be strong

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are what a person or society considers worthwhile.

questions.question: Values are best described as:

options.C: Rules written only in law books
options.D: Standards or principles that people consider desirable and that guide their choices and behaviour

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: They direct what we think is good, right and important.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of values?

options.B: They are learnt through experience and socialisation
options.C: They are inherited genetically and cannot change
options.D: They can be arranged in a hierarchy of importance

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are acquired and can change over time.

questions.question: The saying often used about value education, 'Values are caught, not taught', means that:

options.A: Pupils learn values mainly by observing the example of teachers, parents and society
options.B: Values cannot be learnt at all
options.C: Values must be memorised from books

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Hence the teacher's own conduct is very important.

questions.question: The main objective of value education is:

options.D: The all-round development of character so that the learner becomes a good person and a good citizen

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It develops moral, social, emotional and spiritual aspects of personality.

questions.question: Which committee (1959) was appointed specially to examine religious and moral instruction in educational institutions?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It recommended moral instruction in schools.

questions.question: The Education Commission of 1964–66, which recommended education in moral, social and spiritual values, is popularly known as the:
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It was chaired by Dr D. S. Kothari.

questions.question: The University Education Commission (1948–49), which also stressed moral and spiritual values in higher education, was chaired by:
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It is known as the Radhakrishnan Commission.

questions.question: The National Policy on Education (1986) wanted value education mainly to help:

options.A: Eliminate obscurantism, religious fanaticism, violence, superstition and fatalism

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: It saw value education as a force for social cohesion and national integration.

questions.question: A teacher who is always punctual, honest and fair to all pupils is teaching values mainly through:
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Pupils imitate the behaviour of admired adults.

questions.question: Which method of value education uses stories, dramatisation and discussion of moral dilemmas?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are drawn out of activities rather than preached.

questions.question: Values are said to be 'relative' in the sense that:

options.A: Their priority may differ between persons, cultures and situations
options.B: They are the same for everybody at all times
options.C: They can be measured in rupees
options.D: They depend on height and weight

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Universal values also exist, but the importance given to values varies.

questions.question: Which of the following is an objective of value education?

options.B: Developing respect for others and a sense of social responsibility

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Respect, responsibility and cooperation are core aims.

questions.question:
Match the commission or policy with its year:
a. University Education Commission
b. Sri Prakasa Committee
c. Kothari Commission
d. National Policy on Education

1. 1959
2. 1948–49
3. 1964–66
4. 1986
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: All of them stressed values in education.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Values influence a person's attitudes and behaviour.
II. Values once formed can never change.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values develop and can be modified with experience and education.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The family is the first school of values.
II. The school and the teacher also play a major role in developing values.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Family, school, peers, media and society all shape values.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The teacher's own behaviour is very important in value education.
Reason (R): Children learn values largely by imitating the people they admire.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Values are 'caught' from models.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Value education aims only at improving examination results.
Reason (R): Value education aims at the development of character.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Its aim is character and all-round development; R is true and A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The Kothari Commission recommended education in moral, social and spiritual values.
Reason (R): The Kothari Commission was the first commission appointed after Independence.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: the University Education Commission (1948–49) came first.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Values are learnt and not inborn.
Reason (R): The word 'value' comes from the Latin 'valere'.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values: Meaning, Definition, Objectives and Characteristics
questions.explanation: Both true, but the origin of the word does not explain how values are acquired.

sets.name: 2 · Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values

questions.question: The NCERT document on social, moral and spiritual values in education (1979) listed approximately how many values?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: The list of 83 values is widely quoted in value education courses.

questions.question: Values that are desirable for their own sake, as ends in themselves, are called:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Instrumental values are means to achieve other ends.

questions.question: Milton Rokeach classified values into two types:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Terminal values are desired end-states; instrumental values are modes of behaviour.

questions.question: Eduard Spranger's six types of values are theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: The Allport–Vernon–Lindzey Study of Values is based on Spranger's types.

questions.question: Enjoying music, painting and the beauty of nature reflects which kind of value?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Aesthetic values relate to beauty and art.

questions.question: Standing respectfully when the national anthem is played reflects a:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Patriotism and respect for national symbols are national values.

questions.question: Helping flood victims and taking part in community service reflect:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Social values include cooperation, service and concern for others.

questions.question: Punctuality, self-discipline and cleanliness are usually classed as:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: They relate to an individual's own conduct.

questions.question: Truth, non-violence, peace and love, accepted by people everywhere, are called:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: They are not limited to any one religion, region or culture.

questions.question: The core values mentioned in the Preamble to the Indian Constitution include:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: These are constitutional values every citizen should respect.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the core elements listed in the National Policy on Education (1986)?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Other core elements include India's freedom movement, constitutional obligations, common cultural heritage, egalitarianism, democracy and secularism.

questions.question: Returning a lost wallet with all the money to its owner shows mainly the value of:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Honesty is both a personal and a moral value.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi's life and teaching emphasised above all the values of:
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Satya and ahimsa were the basis of his philosophy.

questions.question: Human values such as compassion and respect for human dignity are values that:

options.B: Apply only to one's own family
options.D: Relate to our common humanity and apply to all people

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: They form the basis of human rights.

questions.question:
Match the value with its category:
a. Patriotism
b. Cooperation
c. Truthfulness
d. Appreciation of beauty

1. Aesthetic
2. Social
3. National
4. Moral
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Categories overlap in practice, but these are the usual classifications.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Intrinsic values are valued for their own sake.
II. Money is usually regarded as an intrinsic value.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Money is valued as a means to other ends, so it is an instrumental (extrinsic) value.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Secularism and democracy are among the values promoted by the Indian Constitution.
II. Protection of the environment is a core element of the National Policy on Education (1986).
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Both are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Truth and non-violence are called universal values.
Reason (R): They are accepted as good in almost all cultures and religions.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Wide acceptance across cultures is what makes a value universal.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Spranger classified values into six types.
Reason (R): Spranger also listed the 83 values in the NCERT document.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: the list of 83 values comes from the NCERT document of 1979.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Social values help people live together in harmony.
Reason (R): Personal values relate to the individual's own conduct.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Classification of Values and NCERT Core Values
questions.explanation: Both true, but R describes personal values and does not explain the role of social values.

questions.question: In the direct method of value education, values are taught:

options.A: Through planned, separate lessons or periods devoted specifically to values

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Moral instruction periods and talks are examples.

questions.question: In the indirect method of value education, values are:

options.B: Taught in a separate period only
options.D: Integrated with the teaching of school subjects and co-curricular activities

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: For example, a science lesson can bring out honesty in recording results.

questions.question: The incidental method of value education means:

options.B: Using events that occur unexpectedly in school or society as occasions to discuss values
options.C: Writing values on the blackboard every day

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: A quarrel in class or a news event can become a value lesson.

questions.question: A pupil returns a lost purse to the office and the headteacher praises this honesty in the morning assembly. This is an example of the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: A real event is used to highlight a value.

questions.question: A history teacher discusses the sacrifices of freedom fighters while teaching the national movement. This illustrates the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Values come through the subject lesson itself.

questions.question: A school has a weekly 'moral science' period where the teacher narrates stories and explains their morals. This is the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It is a separate, planned period for values.

questions.question: Presenting a story with a moral problem and asking pupils what the character should do is the:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It is associated with Kohlberg's work on moral reasoning.

questions.question: In role play for value education, pupils:

options.A: Act out situations to experience different viewpoints and feelings

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It builds empathy and understanding.

questions.question: The 'value clarification' approach (Raths, Harmin and Simon) mainly helps students to:

options.B: Accept the teacher's values without thought
options.C: Become aware of their own values through choosing, prizing and acting

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It focuses on the process of valuing rather than preaching.

questions.question: Celebrating national festivals, observing Environment Day and organising a school cleanliness drive teach values through:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Such activities give practice in citizenship and cooperation.

questions.question: Community service such as visiting an old-age home mainly develops the value of:
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Pupils learn through direct experience of serving others.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the limitation of relying only on the direct method?

options.A: Values may remain as information that is not practised in behaviour
options.D: It takes no time at all

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Values must be experienced and practised, not only explained.

questions.question: School assembly with prayers, thought for the day and news reading is a means of value education because it:

options.B: Gives daily, shared experiences of discipline, reflection and awareness

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: It sets the tone for the school day.

questions.question:
Match the method with its example:
a. Direct method
b. Indirect method
c. Incidental method
d. Role play

1. Bringing out cooperation while teaching a group experiment in science
2. Pupils enact a scene of helping an injured person
3. Discussing a fight in the playground when it happens
4. A separate moral-education period with stories
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Schools generally combine all these methods.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In the indirect method, values are integrated into subject teaching.
II. In the incidental method, the teacher uses events that happen by chance.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Both descriptions are correct.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Value education is effective only when it is examined through written tests.
II. Stories and discussions can be used in value education.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Values show in behaviour; written tests alone cannot measure them.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The incidental method makes value lessons meaningful.
Reason (R): It uses real situations that pupils have just experienced.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Real events make the value concrete and relevant.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Values can be developed only through a separate moral-science period.
Reason (R): Every subject and activity in school can carry values.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Because every subject and activity can carry values, A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Role play helps pupils understand others' feelings.
Reason (R): Role play requires expensive equipment.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – role play needs almost no materials.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Discussing moral dilemmas develops moral reasoning.
Reason (R): Kohlberg proposed three levels of moral development.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Direct, Indirect and Incidental Methods
questions.explanation: Both true, but Kohlberg's levels do not by themselves explain how discussion helps.

sets.name: 2 · Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers

questions.question: Mass media such as television, newspapers and the Internet influence values mainly because they:

options.D: Reach large numbers of people and present models of behaviour

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Children often imitate what they see on screen.

questions.question: A negative influence of media on children's values can be:

options.D: Exposure to violence, consumerism and stereotypes

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Guidance helps children view media critically.

questions.question: A positive use of media in value education is:

options.A: Letting pupils watch any content without guidance
options.C: Showing a documentary on environmental conservation followed by discussion

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Discussion turns viewing into learning.

questions.question: 'Media literacy' means the ability to:

options.B: Access, analyse, evaluate and create media messages critically

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: It protects children against misinformation and manipulation.

questions.question: Checking whether a message forwarded on social media is true before sharing it shows the value of:
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Fake news can cause real harm.

questions.question: Cyberbullying is best prevented in school by:

options.C: Teaching respectful online behaviour, empathy and how to report problems

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Digital citizenship is part of modern value education.

questions.question: The most important role of the teacher in value education is to:

options.A: Be a role model whose own conduct shows the values taught

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Pupils notice whether a teacher practises what they preach.

questions.question: A teacher treats all pupils equally regardless of caste, religion or gender. This models the value of:
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Equal treatment is also a constitutional value.

questions.question: Creating a classroom climate where pupils feel safe to express opinions promotes the values of:

options.B: Freedom of expression and mutual respect

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: A democratic classroom teaches democracy by practice.

questions.question: Involving parents in value education is important because:

options.A: Values learnt at school are reinforced (or weakened) at home
options.B: Values are learnt only at home

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Home and school must work together.

questions.question: The NCERT (2012) document on values in schools is titled:

options.C: Education for Values in Schools – A Framework

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: It advocates a whole-school approach to values.

questions.question: A 'whole-school approach' to value education means:

options.A: Values are reflected in the school's policies, climate, relationships and all activities
options.D: Values are taught once a year

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Everyone in the school contributes.

questions.question: A teacher who comes late regularly but lectures pupils on punctuality is likely to:

options.D: Fail to develop the value, because the example contradicts the words

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Values are caught more than they are taught.

questions.question:
Match the medium with a value-education use:
a. Newspaper
b. Film
c. Radio
d. Internet

1. Listening to an educational broadcast programme
2. A news-reading and discussion session in assembly
3. Viewing and discussing a story of courage
4. Researching a social issue online for a project
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: All media can serve value education with guidance.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Media can influence children's values both positively and negatively.
II. The teacher should help pupils evaluate media messages critically.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: That is the purpose of media literacy.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The teacher's behaviour has little effect on pupils' values.
II. Parents also shape children's values.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: The teacher is one of the strongest models for pupils.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Teachers should model the values they teach.
Reason (R): Pupils learn values largely by imitating people they respect.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Modelling is the most powerful method.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): All media content is harmful to children.
Reason (R): Media can present violence and stereotypes.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Some content is harmful, but much is educational; A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Media literacy should be part of value education today.
Reason (R): Media literacy means avoiding all use of the Internet.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – media literacy means using media critically, not avoiding it.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A democratic classroom helps develop democratic values.
Reason (R): The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Values and Media, and the Role of Teachers
questions.explanation: Both true, but the date does not explain why a democratic classroom develops those values.

sets.name: 1 · Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism

questions.question: Something that is good in itself, valued as an end and not for anything else, has:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Happiness and virtue are common examples of intrinsic goods.

questions.question: Something that is good because it helps us get something else has:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Money is good as a means to food, shelter, education and so on.

questions.question: Which of these is usually given as an example of an external (instrumental) good?
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Its value lies in what it can buy or achieve.

questions.question: Kant held that the only thing good without any qualification is:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Opening idea of Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785).

questions.question: Hedonism is the ethical theory that:

options.C: Duty for duty's sake is the highest good

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). From Greek hēdonē, 'pleasure'.

questions.question: Psychological hedonism holds that:

options.A: By nature, people always seek pleasure and avoid pain
options.B: People ought to seek the pleasure of others

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Ethical hedonism says what people OUGHT to seek; psychological hedonism describes what they DO seek.

questions.question: The Greek philosopher associated with egoistic, sensual hedonism (the Cyrenaic school) is:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). He valued the intense pleasures of the present moment.

questions.question: Epicurus taught that the highest pleasure is:

options.C: Freedom from pain in the body and from disturbance in the mind (ataraxia)

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: He preferred simple, lasting, refined pleasures.

questions.question: Utilitarianism, a form of universalistic hedonism, judges an action right if it produces:

options.A: Obedience to rules regardless of results
options.C: The greatest pleasure for the doer only
options.D: The greatest happiness of the greatest number

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Associated with Jeremy Bentham and J. S. Mill.

questions.question: Jeremy Bentham's hedonic (felicific) calculus measures pleasures by their:

options.A: Quantity – intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fecundity, purity and extent

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Bentham: 'quantity of pleasure being equal, pushpin is as good as poetry'.

questions.question: J. S. Mill differed from Bentham by holding that pleasures differ in:

options.B: Quality as well as quantity – higher (intellectual) pleasures are better than lower (bodily) ones

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.'

questions.question: The 'paradox of hedonism' states that:

options.A: Pleasure and pain are the same
options.C: Those who chase pleasure directly often fail to find it; it comes as a by-product of other pursuits

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Discussed by Henry Sidgwick.

questions.question: The Indian school that held 'as long as you live, live happily' (yāvat jīvet sukhaṃ jīvet) is:
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). A materialist, hedonistic school.

questions.question: For Aristotle, the highest human good is:

options.B: Eudaimonia – flourishing or well-being achieved through a life of virtue

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: It is a life of activity in accordance with virtue, not mere pleasure.

questions.question: A common criticism of hedonism is that:

options.A: It ignores values such as duty, justice and character, which we prize even when they bring no pleasure
options.C: It is too difficult to understand

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Critics such as Kant and the idealists stressed duty and self-realisation.

questions.question:
Match the thinker with the idea:
a. Aristippus
b. Epicurus
c. Bentham
d. Mill

1. Intense pleasure of the moment
2. Freedom from pain and mental calm
3. Pleasures differ in quality
4. Quantitative hedonic calculus
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Thinker-idea matching is common in value-education sections.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Money is an example of external goodness.
II. Happiness is usually considered an internal good.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Money is a means; happiness is sought for its own sake.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Bentham measured pleasures by quality alone.
II. Mill accepted that some pleasures are higher than others.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Bentham measured quantity; Mill added quality.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Utilitarianism is called universalistic hedonism.
Reason (R): It aims at the happiness of all people affected, not only of the doer.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: Egoistic hedonism seeks only one's own pleasure.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): According to hedonism, knowledge is the highest good.
Reason (R): Hedonism treats pleasure as the highest good.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Internal and External Goodness, and Hedonism
questions.explanation: A contradicts the theory itself; R states it correctly.

sets.name: 2 · Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution

questions.question: Moral pluralism holds that:

options.A: There are many genuine moral values or duties that cannot all be reduced to a single one
options.C: There is no right or wrong
options.D: Every culture has exactly the same rules

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Monism, by contrast, reduces all value to one supreme principle.

questions.question: The philosopher who proposed several 'prima facie duties' (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence) is:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). A classic statement of moral pluralism (The Right and the Good, 1930).

questions.question: In moral pluralism, when two duties conflict (e.g. keeping a promise vs helping someone in danger), a person must:

options.B: Use judgement to decide which duty is weightier in that situation
options.C: Always follow the first duty learned

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Ross called the winning duty one's 'actual' duty in that case.

questions.question: The view that the single highest good is pleasure is an example of:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Pluralists accept several independent goods.

questions.question: Which of the following is a moral quality (virtue)?
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Moral qualities concern character and conduct.

questions.question: Plato's four cardinal virtues are:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Each corresponds to a part of the soul or a class in the ideal state.

questions.question: Self-control, especially over desires and appetites, is called:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Aristotle placed it as the mean between excess and insensibility.

questions.question: The self-realisation (self-evolution) theory says that the highest good is:

options.D: The full development of a person's true self – intellectual, emotional and moral

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Associated with Hegel, T. H. Green and F. H. Bradley; in India with ātma-sākṣātkāra.

questions.question: Which statement best expresses self-evolution as a moral ideal?

options.B: A person grows morally by steadily developing good qualities and controlling lower impulses
options.C: Morality is only about external rewards
options.D: A person is born perfect and cannot change

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Education aims at this all-round growth.

questions.question: For Mahatma Gandhi, the ultimate aim of life was:

options.B: Self-realisation – seeing God (Truth) face to face

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). From the introduction to his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth.

questions.question: Aristotle described a virtue as:

options.B: An inborn quality that cannot be learned
options.C: A mean between two extremes – excess and deficiency

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Courage is the mean between rashness and cowardice.

questions.question: Courage, according to Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, lies between:
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Rashness is excess; cowardice is deficiency.

questions.question: Moral qualities are developed in school children mainly through:

options.C: Example of teachers, practice in daily life and reflection on experiences

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Values are 'caught' as much as 'taught'.

questions.question: The Bhagavad Gita's teaching of nishkāma karma means:

options.D: Doing one's duty without attachment to its fruits

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Contrasts with hedonism, which judges acts by the pleasure they bring.

questions.question:
Match the theory with its central idea:
a. Hedonism
b. Moral pluralism
c. Self-realisation
d. Kantian ethics

1. Full development of the true self
2. Many independent duties and values
3. Pleasure is the highest good
4. Duty done from a good will
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Theory-idea matching.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Moral pluralism accepts that duties can conflict.
II. Moral pluralism reduces every value to pleasure.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Reducing everything to pleasure is hedonistic monism.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Wisdom, courage, temperance and justice are Plato's cardinal virtues.
II. Self-realisation theory sees moral life as growth of the whole personality.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Both are standard textbook statements.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): According to the self-realisation theory, mere pleasure cannot be the highest good.
Reason (R): The theory sees the highest good in the harmonious development of all sides of the self.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Pleasure satisfies only one side of human nature.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Virtues can be developed through practice.
Reason (R): Aristotle said that we become just by doing just acts.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Habituation builds character.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.subject: Moral Pluralism, Moral Qualities and Self-evolution
questions.explanation: Bentham devised the hedonic calculus; Kant spoke of the good will; Plato listed the cardinal virtues.

topics.name: Rules and Principles of Human Behaviour

questions.question: Which philosophy of education condemns enforced discipline and advocates social discipline based on child's interests?
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Pragmatists (John Dewey) want discipline to grow out of purposeful, shared social activity that interests the child; naturalism relies on the natural consequences of acts. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)

questions.question: Rules of behaviour that a society expects its members to follow, and that are enforced by approval or disapproval, are called:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Folkways, mores, customs and laws are kinds of social norms.

questions.question: Norms whose violation brings strong moral condemnation (for example, rules against theft) are called:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: W. G. Sumner divided norms into folkways (everyday customs) and mores (morally important rules).

questions.question: Ordinary everyday customs such as ways of greeting or dressing, whose violation brings only mild disapproval, are:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Breaking a folkway is seen as odd or rude, not as immoral.

questions.question: The difference between a law and a moral rule is that a law is:

options.D: Enforced by the State with legal penalties

questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Moral rules are enforced by conscience and social approval; laws by courts and the State.

questions.question: The 'Golden Rule' of human behaviour says:

options.A: Treat others as you would like them to treat you

questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: It is found in almost every religion and ethical tradition.

questions.question: Kant's categorical imperative asks us to act only on that maxim which we can will to become a:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Kant also said: treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means.

questions.question: The principle of 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number' belongs to:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). It judges actions by their consequences.

questions.question: A rule of behaviour that a person follows because he has accepted it as right, without needing an outside authority, shows:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Piaget: young children show heteronomous morality (rules come from adults); older children move to autonomous morality.

questions.question: According to Kohlberg, a person who obeys rules mainly to avoid punishment is at the:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Stage 1 – punishment and obedience orientation.

questions.question: In Kohlberg's theory, 'good boy – nice girl' orientation and 'law and order' orientation belong to the:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Stages 3 and 4 – behaviour is guided by the approval of others and by respect for social rules.

questions.question: The highest stage in Kohlberg's moral development, where a person follows self-chosen ethical principles of justice, is:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Stage 6; stage 5 is the social-contract orientation. Both are post-conventional.

questions.question: The inner sense that tells a person what is right and wrong and makes him feel guilty after wrong action is:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Freud linked it to the superego.

questions.question: In a school, rules are most likely to be followed willingly when they are:

options.A: Few, clear, fair and made with the pupils' participation

questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Democratic discipline builds self-discipline.

questions.question: Which principle says that a person should be free to act as he wishes as long as he does not harm others?
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Mill set it out in 'On Liberty' (1859).

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Rules make social life orderly and predictable.
II. Moral principles are more general than rules and help us judge which rules are right.
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Principles (truth, justice, non-violence) lie behind particular rules.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Discipline imposed only through fear rarely produces lasting good behaviour.
Reason (R): Behaviour controlled by fear tends to disappear when the authority is absent.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: That is why educators stress self-discipline and inner motivation.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Customs and traditions are the same in all societies.
Reason (R): Norms of behaviour are learnt through socialisation.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: Customs differ between societies and over time; R is true.

questions.question: The process by which a child learns the norms, values and behaviour patterns of his society is:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Family is the primary agency; school, peers and media follow.

questions.question: Gandhiji's principles of human behaviour – truth and non-violence – are known as:
questions.subject: Rules, Norms and Moral Principles
questions.explanation: He called his life 'My Experiments with Truth'.

questions.question: Individual behaviour is the result of the interaction of:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Woodworth: behaviour = f(heredity × environment).

questions.question: Kurt Lewin expressed behaviour as B = f(P, E), where P and E stand for:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Lewin's field theory: behaviour depends on the person and his psychological environment (life space).

questions.question: Which of the following is a biological (internal) factor affecting behaviour?
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Hormones from the thyroid, adrenal and other glands affect energy, mood and emotion.

questions.question: Over-secretion of the thyroid hormone usually makes a person:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Under-secretion causes sluggishness and, in children, cretinism.

questions.question: The primary social group that has the earliest and deepest influence on a child's behaviour is the:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: C. H. Cooley called family and play groups primary groups.

questions.question: During adolescence the most powerful influence on behaviour such as dress, speech and interests usually comes from the:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Conformity to peers is strongest in early adolescence.

questions.question: Behaviour that is learnt by observing and imitating a model is explained by:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Bandura's Bobo-doll experiment showed children imitating aggression.

questions.question: Values, attitudes and beliefs affect behaviour because they:

options.B: Act as inner guides for choosing actions

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: An attitude has cognitive, affective and behavioural components.

questions.question: A need that, according to Maslow, must be met before a person seeks esteem and self-actualisation is:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Maslow's hierarchy: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation.

questions.question: A child who is repeatedly scolded and compared with others is likely to develop:

options.B: Low self-esteem and withdrawal or aggression

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Self-concept is shaped by how significant others treat the child.

questions.question: Which of the following is a cultural factor affecting behaviour?

options.D: Customs, religion and language of the community

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Culture defines what behaviour is acceptable.

questions.question: Emotional stress and frustration commonly lead to:

options.A: Defence mechanisms such as rationalisation, projection or displacement

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Defence mechanisms protect the self from anxiety.

questions.question: Blaming others for one's own faults is the defence mechanism called:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Sublimation channels energy into socially approved activity.

questions.question: Giving a socially acceptable but false reason for one's behaviour (e.g. 'the grapes are sour') is:
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: The 'sour grapes' and 'sweet lemon' mechanisms are forms of rationalisation.

questions.question: The term 'temperament' refers to:

options.A: A person's characteristic emotional nature, partly inborn

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Children may be 'easy', 'difficult' or 'slow to warm up' (Thomas and Chess).

questions.question: Which factor affects a pupil's classroom behaviour the most directly?

options.A: The colour of the school building
options.D: The teacher's personality, attitude and methods

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). A warm, fair, democratic teacher reduces indiscipline.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Heredity sets the limits of development.
II. Environment decides how far those limits are reached.
questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Both act together; neither alone explains behaviour.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Two children of the same family may behave very differently.
Reason (R): Individual differences arise from differences in heredity, environment and experience.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Even siblings differ in heredity (except identical twins) and in their experiences.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Behaviour is fixed at birth and cannot be changed.
Reason (R): Education aims at bringing desirable changes in behaviour.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: Behaviour can be modified through learning; R is the usual definition of education.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the same person behaves differently in different situations?

options.A: Behaviour depends on the situation as well as on the person

questions.subject: Factors Affecting Individual Behaviour
questions.explanation: This is the person–situation interaction view.

questions.question: The principle that a moral rule must apply equally to everyone in similar circumstances is called:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). If an act is right for me, it is right for anyone in the same situation.

questions.question: Kant's test 'Act only on that maxim which you can at the same time will to become a universal law' expresses:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Kant called it the first formulation of the categorical imperative.

questions.question: Kant argued that lying is wrong because:

options.D: If everyone lied, trust would collapse, so the maxim cannot be universalised

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Kant judged acts by duty, not consequences.

questions.question: The view that morality is grounded in reason, so that every rational being can know what is right, is called:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Kant is the leading rationalist moral philosopher.

questions.question: Aristotle described the human being as a:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). He held that a good life is one lived according to reason and virtue.

questions.question: David Hume's famous statement 'Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions' means:

options.C: Reason guides us to goals set by our desires; it does not by itself move us to act

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Hume is a sentimentalist, contrasted with Kant's rationalism.

questions.question: A categorical imperative differs from a hypothetical imperative in that it:

options.C: Depends on a goal such as 'if you want to pass, study'

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Hypothetical imperatives say 'If you want X, do Y'.

questions.question: Kant's 'formula of humanity' says that we should:

options.C: Treat humanity always as an end and never merely as a means

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Using people merely as tools is wrong.

questions.question: Moral judgements are said to be 'impartial' when:

options.A: Everyone's interests are given equal weight, without favouring oneself

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Impartiality is closely linked with universality.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of applying the principle of universality in a classroom?

options.A: The same rule on late submission applies to every student
options.B: Rules change for the teacher's favourite

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Fairness to all builds trust.

questions.question: The 'Golden Rule' – treat others as you would like to be treated – is closely related to:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). It appears in almost every religious tradition.

questions.question: The view that what is morally right depends entirely on what each culture approves is:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Universalists argue some principles (e.g. against cruelty) hold for all cultures.

questions.question: Rationality in moral behaviour mainly means:

options.A: Acting on good reasons that can be explained and defended to others

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Moral reasoning weighs facts and principles.

questions.question: Kohlberg's highest stage, in which a person follows self-chosen universal ethical principles, shows:

options.A: Morality based on reason and universality

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Stage 6 – universal ethical principles orientation.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A universal moral rule allows exceptions only for oneself.
II. Universality requires treating similar cases alike.
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Making exceptions for oneself violates universality.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): For Kant, an act done only out of fear of punishment has no moral worth.
Reason (R): Kant held that an act has moral worth only when done from duty.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Kant valued the 'good will' acting from duty.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Hume held that reason alone is the source of morality.
Reason (R): Hume thought moral distinctions come from sentiments (feelings) of approval and disapproval.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Hume grounded morality in sentiment, not reason alone.

questions.question:
Match:
a. Kant
b. Hume
c. Aristotle
d. Mill

1. Virtue and the rational animal
2. Utilitarianism
3. Reason as slave of passions
4. Categorical imperative
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Philosopher–idea matching is common.

questions.question: A person returns extra change given by mistake at a shop because 'if everyone kept such money, honesty would disappear'. This reasoning uses:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: Asking 'what if everyone did this?' is a universalisability test.

questions.question: The view that moral principles bind all rational beings regardless of time and place is:
questions.subject: Universality, Rationality and Morality
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Human-rights declarations rest on universalist ideas.

sets.name: 2 · Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest

questions.question: Psychological egoism is the theory that:

options.A: People ought to act from self-interest
options.B: All people always act from self-interest

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). It is a descriptive claim about how people do act.

questions.question: Ethical (moral) egoism is the theory that:

options.B: Each person ought to pursue his or her own self-interest exclusively

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: It is a normative claim about how people should act.

questions.question: The philosopher who described the life of man in the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short' and is associated with egoism is:
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). He argued that people accept a social contract for self-protection (Leviathan, 1651).

questions.question: The writer who defended 'rational self-interest' and called selfishness a virtue in 'The Virtue of Selfishness' was:
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Her philosophy is called Objectivism.

questions.question: Rational self-interest means:

options.B: Doing whatever one feels like at the moment
options.C: Pursuing one's long-term interests guided by reason, not by every passing impulse

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). A rational egoist may keep promises because it pays in the long run.

questions.question: Bishop Joseph Butler criticised psychological egoism by arguing that:

options.A: We often desire things (like others' welfare) for their own sake, and pleasure follows from getting them

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: This is the 'paradox of hedonism' argument.

questions.question: Behaviour aimed at the welfare of others without expecting reward is called:
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). The term was coined by Auguste Comte.

questions.question: A common objection to ethical egoism is that it:

options.D: Cannot resolve conflicts of interest fairly and ignores the equal worth of others

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Rachels argues it makes an arbitrary distinction between oneself and others.

questions.question: Which idea, often raised against egoism and hedonism, says that people who aim directly at their own pleasure often fail to find it?
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Happiness usually comes as a by-product of other pursuits (Sidgwick).

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of enlightened (rational) self-interest?

options.A: Giving away all savings to strangers
options.D: A shopkeeper is honest because it builds customers' trust and long-term business

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Honesty here serves long-term interest.

questions.question: Adam Smith's idea that individuals pursuing their own interest in a market can benefit society is known as:
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). He also wrote 'The Theory of Moral Sentiments' on sympathy.

questions.question: The 'prisoner's dilemma' shows that:

options.C: When each person pursues narrow self-interest, both can end up worse off than if they cooperated
options.D: Selfishness always gives the best result

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: It is used to explain the value of trust and rules.

questions.question: According to Indian ethical traditions such as the Bhagavad Gita, the ideal is:

options.D: Nishkama karma – doing one's duty without selfish attachment to results

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). It contrasts sharply with ethical egoism.

questions.question: Moral egoism differs from rational self-interest mainly in that moral egoism:

options.A: Claims self-interest is the only moral standard, while rational self-interest stresses long-term, reasoned pursuit of interests

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Many rational egoists accept cooperation as serving self-interest.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Psychological egoism is a descriptive theory.
II. Ethical egoism is a normative theory.
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: One describes what people do; the other prescribes what they ought to do.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A teacher who helps a weak student after school without any reward shows altruistic behaviour.
Reason (R): Altruism is concern for the welfare of others.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Value education aims to develop such concern.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Psychological egoism is proved by the fact that people feel pleasure after helping others.
Reason (R): Butler argued that pleasure is the result of satisfying a desire for others' good, not its aim.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Feeling pleasure does not show that pleasure was the motive – R is the standard reply.

questions.question:
Match:

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). Thinker–theory matching.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relation between rationality and morality according to most moral philosophers?

options.A: Moral rules can be justified by reasons that every rational person can accept
options.B: Morality has nothing to do with reason

questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: Contractarians and Kantians both link morality with reason.

questions.question: The 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment, which asks us to choose rules without knowing our own position in society, was proposed by:
questions.subject: Moral Egoism, Altruism and Rational Self-interest
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (GPSTR / TET value education). It aims at impartial, universal principles of justice (A Theory of Justice, 1971).
